Dynamic population modelling demonstration with Julia

Background

We will use an example from the book A Practical Handbook for Population Viability Analysis (Morris et al. 1999).

This example demonstrates possible code and techniques to perform population viability analysis using population Projection Matrix Models using the example in Box 4.1.

A Projection Matrix Model combines life-history data (transitions between different life stages) and abundance estimates to project possible future outcomes for a population. This example uses data on American Oystercatchers.

Julia packages and environments

Julia uses environments to install and manage different packages that are used in a project. This is accessed by pressing ] in the Julia terminal (return using Ctrl + c).

Required package names are recorded in the Project.toml file. Julia and package versions are recorded in the Manifest.toml file. These are machine-edited files that do not need to be edited manually.

Package management commands: - activate : activate a new environment in the current folder. This creates Project.toml and Manifest.toml files to create an environment. - instantiate : setup an environment from existing *.toml files. This is used if you clone a project from GitHub for example. - add : Add a package (can include versions or GitHub repositories). - rm : Remove a package from the environment. - status : See current environment status (packages and julia version). - pin : Set the version of a package(s) to be stable. This is useful for reproducibility and ensuring consistent package version use.

Example

Use the REPL (terminal) to activate the package manager, and add DataFrames package. ] -> add DataFrames

Then the package can be loaded in the session.

using DataFrames # `using` is similar to `library` in R.
using Statistics # provides statistical functions such as `median`, `quantile` etc.

# You can also use `import` instead of `using`

Step 1: Stage-structured matrix

The first step of using a Projected Matrix Model is to create a transition matrix between components of the target population.

  • Matrix rows and columns represent stages of the population of interest
  • Values represent the rate of transition (annual or other temporal scale) between each combination of size classes
  • Columns represent the stage transitioning FROM and rows represent the stage transitioning TO

To do this in Julia we create an object of type Matrix{Float64}.

# This is a square matrix where values represent transitions between population stages
# This matrix is in the format:
#                                   FROM
#                   Juveniles   Sub-adults  Adults
#       Juveniles       0           0           0.054
#   TO: Sub-adults      0.665       0           0
#       Adults          0           0.724       0.95

# There are multiple ways to create this matrix
# Simplest: Creating a matrix of Float64 values directly
ao_stage_matrix = [
    0      0      0.054;
    0.665   0      0;
    0      0.724  0.95
]

# Creating a matrix from DataFrame columns
ao_stages = DataFrame(
    to = ["juveniles", "sub_adults", "adults"], # Vector of strings
    juveniles = [0, 0.665, 0], # Vector of Float64
    sub_adults = [0, 0, 0.724],
    adults = [0.054, 0, 0.95]
)
# From selection of columns
ao_stage_matrix = Matrix(ao_stages[:, [:juveniles, :sub_adults, :adults]])

# From 'inverse' selection of columns
ao_stage_matrix = Matrix(ao_stages[:, Not(:to)])

ao_stage_matrix
3×3 Matrix{Float64}:
 0.0    0.0    0.054
 0.665  0.0    0.0
 0.0    0.724  0.95

Step 2: Initial population conditions

Step 2 is to setup the initial population conditions in a population state vector. This holds current values for the abundance of each stage (i.e. N0).

# Initial population state in the format
#       J  S-A  A
N_0 = [40, 50, 60]
3-element Vector{Int64}:
 40
 50
 60

Step 3: Matrix multiplication projection

The third step in projection matrix modelling is to project the population state using transition values.

N_1 = ao_stage_matrix * N_0
3-element Vector{Float64}:
  3.2399999999999998
 26.6
 93.19999999999999

Projection Matrix Modelling

Now we can turn the matrix multiplication into a model function that will project the population for a determined number of years.

Creating a function in julia uses the function, return, and end keywords.

function project_model(
    initial_conditions::Vector{<:Real},
    transition_parameter_matrix::Matrix{Float64},
    years::Int64
)::Matrix{Float64}
    # Create an empty array to hold the results for the model
    n_components = length(initial_conditions)
    proj_results = fill(NaN, n_components, years + 1)

    # Allocate the initial conditions to the initial year column
    proj_results[:, 1] = initial_conditions
    
    # Now loop through each year and combine the transition matrix with the previous year's population state
    for year in 1:years
        proj_results[:, year + 1] = transition_parameter_matrix * proj_results[:, year]
    end

    return proj_results
end
project_model (generic function with 1 method)

Visualisation

Now we can project the population model for 100 years and visualise the projections.

projections_100t = project_model(N_0, ao_stage_matrix, 99)
3×100 Matrix{Float64}:
 40.0   3.24    5.0328    5.82111  …   0.656571   0.641618   0.627005
 50.0  26.6     2.1546    3.34681      0.446796   0.43662    0.426676
 60.0  93.2   107.798   103.968       11.8818    11.6112    11.3468

There are two main ecosystems for visualisation in julia: Plots.jl and Makie.jl

I will focus on Makie.jl for this session. Makie.jl is an ecosystem that contains a backend package (you do not need to install) and several front-end packages (that you will install) depending on your use case.

  • CairoMakie.jl is great for fast, high resolution, publication quality plotting.
  • GLMakie.jl is great for plotting interatively (zoom, navigate) while developing plots.
  • Makie.jl also interacts with AlgebraOfGraphics.jl which is a plotting package similar to ggplot2 in R.

Plotting with base Makie.jl for fine-scale control

Using Makie.jl (with CairoMakie or GLMakie frontend) allows more fine-scale control, and more plot types (e.g. animations, 3D plots) but can take more time to develop compared to AlgebraOfGraphics.jl.

using CairoMakie

# Basic plotting:
fig = series(projections_100t)

# Finer control plotting:
fig = Figure(size = (650, 450), fontsize=12)
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel="Abundance", ylabel="Timestep")

series!(ax, projections_100t, color=[:red, :green, :blue]) # Adding control of colours
legend_entries = [
    PolyElement(; color=:red),
    PolyElement(; color=:green),
    PolyElement(; color=:blue)
]
Legend(fig[2, 1], legend_entries, ["juveniles", "sub_adults", "adults"]; tell_width=false, tell_height=false, orientation=:horizontal)

fig

Plotting algebraically with AlgebraOfGraphics.jl for speed

AlgebraOfGraphics.jl (AoG) allows you to get quickly get from DataFrame to a figure, similar to how ggplot2 works, but has fewer plot types available than base Makie.jl. AoG uses Makie.jl behind the scenes, so all plots can be custom modified using Makie.jl syntax to add legends, colour bars etc.

# using GLMakie # Would usually be required if not loaded already
using AlgebraOfGraphics

# To work with AlgebraOfGraphics.jl we need a DataFrame, similar to ggplot2 in R
# To do this we transpose the matrix and add column names
projection_df = DataFrame(Matrix(projections_100t'), ["juveniles", "sub_adults", "adults"])
projection_df.timestep = 1:nrow(projection_df)

# Convert this to a long-format `stack` is equivalent to `pivot_longer` (`unstack` is equivalent to `pivot_wider`)
projection_df = stack(projection_df, [:juveniles, :sub_adults, :adults], :timestep; variable_name=:stage, value_name=:abundance)

# Plotting with AlgebraOfGraphics
# mapping() is equivalent to `aes` in ggplot() functions
# visual() determines the type of plot
# draw() renders the output, and applies additional settings e.g. figure sizes, layouts, fontsize etc.
projection_lines = data(projection_df) * mapping(:timestep, :abundance, color=:stage) * visual(Lines)
fig = draw(projection_lines)

Example of stochastic simulation and plotting workflow with multiple dispatch

Transition rates may be affected by stochastic environmental variation, affecting population projections.

In this example we incorporate stochasticity by drawing our rate values from continuous distributions. For simplicity, we will use uniform distributions of rate values loosely based on the values from Morris et al. (1999).

We will only vary the fecundity rates (adult to juvenile transition) and adult survival rates (adult to adult transition).

The Distributions.jl package provides functionality for statistical distributions and sampling. We use Dirac() to just sample a constant value (i.e. keep values from Morris et al.) and Uniform(a, b) to specify a uniform distribution between values a and b.

We format these distributions in a matrix. We then use Julia broadcasting. Broadcasting runs a function over each element in an array. This functionality uses a . before function brackets and the same as using a for loop or map function to sample each of the distributions in our object.

Creating distributions

using Distributions

# Create a matrix of distributions for our sampling
# This is not the most efficient way to sample matrices since most of the values are constant,
# but here we use it to demonstrate broadcasting

dist_stage_matrix = UnivariateDistribution[
    Dirac(0.0)      Dirac(0.0)      Uniform(0.054 - 0.05, 0.054 + 0.05)
    Dirac(0.665)    Dirac(0.0)      Dirac(0.0)
    Dirac(0.0)      Dirac(0.724)    Uniform(0.95 - 0.05, 0.95 + 0.05)
]

# Formatting the distributions as a matrix ensures that when drawn with rand.(), we keep the matrix format
rand.(dist_stage_matrix)
3×3 Matrix{Float64}:
 0.0    0.0    0.0230455
 0.665  0.0    0.0
 0.0    0.724  0.976306

We can now sample values for many different model projections.

Multiple dispatch

Multiple dispatch is a feature that lets you define multiple methods for a single function depending on the type of the arguments given. This means that functions can have different behaviour depending on the type of arguments.

Currently our function project_model() has one method, where the transition_parameter_matrix argument is of the type Matrix{Float64} (so this will not work with our distribution matrix).

We can use multiple dispatch to create a second method for this function so that different behaviour is used when the type of transition_parameter_matrix is Matrix{UnivariateDistribution}.

Defining a new method for the function is the same how we defined a function earlier.

function project_model(
    initial_conditions::Vector{<:Real},
    transition_parameter_matrix::Matrix{UnivariateDistribution},
    years::Int64
)::Matrix{Float64}
    # Create an empty array to hold the results for the model
    n_components = length(initial_conditions)
    proj_results = fill(NaN, (n_components, years + 1))

    # Allocate the initial conditions to the initial year column
    proj_results[:, 1] = initial_conditions
    
    # Now loop through each year and combine the transition matrix with the previous year's population state
    for year in 1:years
        proj_results[:, year + 1] = rand.(transition_parameter_matrix) * @view proj_results[:, year]
    end

    return proj_results
end
project_model (generic function with 2 methods)

Simulations

Now we can use this new model method to project many stochastic simulations of our PMM and visualise the results. We still use N_0 as our initial population state, and model 99 years.

# We will run the model for 100,000 simulations
n_stages = length(N_0)
n_sim = 100000
years = 99

# Setup results array
stochastic_results = fill(NaN, n_stages, years + 1, n_sim)

# Use a for loop to perform each simulation.
# This could easily be parallelised using the FLoops.jl package by adding @floop before `for`
for i in 1:n_sim
    stochastic_results[:, :, i] = project_model(N_0, dist_stage_matrix, years)
end

Plotting

To understand how environmental variation translates to population variation we might plot individual timeseries. Here we will plot 2,000 out of the 100,000 timeseries for speed.

fig = Figure(size=(650, 450))
ax = Axis(fig[1,1], xlabel="Timestep", ylabel="Abundance")

idx = rand(1:100000, 2000)
colours = Makie.wong_colors()[1:3] # Use the same colour palette as AlgebraOfGraphics.jl

for i in idx
    series!(ax, stochastic_results[:, :, i], color=map(x -> (x, 0.3), colours))
end

# Add the original deterministic projections on top
series!(ax, projections_100t, solid_color=:black)

legend_entries = [
    PolyElement(; color=colours[1]),
    PolyElement(; color=colours[2]),
    PolyElement(; color=colours[3])
]
Legend(
    fig[2, 1], 
    legend_entries, 
    ["juveniles", "sub_adults", "adults"]; 
    tell_width=false, 
    tell_height=false, 
    orientation=:horizontal
)

fig
